title: WE REBUKE THE DEVIL LOUDLY… BUT WHY ARE WE SO QUIET ABOUT OUR OWN PRIDE?
paragraphs: WE REBUKE THE DEVIL LOUDLY… BUT WHY ARE WE SO QUIET ABOUT OUR OWN PRIDE?

What if the enemy you keep blaming isn't responsible for the very thing destroying your relationships, hardening your heart, and keeping you from repentance? What if the spiritual battle you've been fighting has exposed something you never wanted to confront… yourself?
There is something deeply unsettling about a Christian who can recognize the devil's schemes in everyone else's life but cannot recognize pride in their own heart.
We can rebuke Satan with authority.
We can declare that no weapon formed against us shall prosper.
We can pray against every attack, every opposition, every spiritual stronghold.
But ask us to apologize?
Suddenly, we have a hundred explanations.
Ask us to admit we were wrong?
Suddenly, we feel misunderstood.
Ask us to forgive someone who wounded our ego?
Suddenly, we need more time to pray.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that we can do all of this while genuinely believing we are standing for God.
Read that again.
Because sometimes the greatest obstacle to our spiritual growth isn't an attack from the enemy.
It's the pride we have mistaken for spiritual strength.
And before you decide this message is for someone else, consider one uncomfortable possibility.
What if the person God wants to confront through these words is the person reading them?
I remember how easily we Christians can say, "The devil is attacking my family."
But sometimes the family isn't falling apart because Satan has somehow overpowered the home.
Sometimes a husband refuses to listen because he believes being the head of the household means never admitting he is wrong.
Sometimes a wife has been carrying resentment for years because forgiveness feels too much like surrendering her right to be angry.
Sometimes parents demand respect from their children while refusing to acknowledge the wounds their own words have caused.
Sometimes children justify dishonoring their parents because they believe their pain excuses every response.
Sometimes a church friendship dies, not because the devil won a supernatural battle, but because two believers would rather lose each other than lose an argument.
And yes, spiritual warfare is real.
Scripture never tells us to dismiss the devil or ignore his schemes.
But Scripture also never gives us permission to blame Satan for sins we refuse to confess.
James 4:7 says:
"Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you." (KJV)
Notice the order.
Submit to God.
Then resist the devil.
We love the second command because it sounds powerful.
We struggle with the first because it requires surrender.
In the original Greek, the word translated "submit" is ὑποτάγητε (hypotagēte), from the verb hypotassō, meaning to place oneself under authority or become subject to another.
James is not presenting spiritual resistance as a performance of religious confidence.
He is calling believers to come under God's authority.
And the surrounding passage makes his meaning even more uncomfortable.
James 4:6 declares:
"God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble." (KJV)
The Greek word translated "proud" is ὑπερηφάνοις (hyperēphanois), referring to the arrogant or haughty.
And the word translated "resisteth" is ἀντιτάσσεται (antitassetai), expressing active opposition.
Think about that.
We can spend an entire evening praying against spiritual opposition while refusing to humble ourselves before the God who opposes pride.
Not because God has stopped loving us.
Not because grace has disappeared.
But because the very pride we are defending is contrary to the humility through which we receive His grace.
What a terrifying contradiction.
We want God to defeat our enemies while we protect the sin He is calling us to surrender.
And the tragedy is that pride rarely announces itself honestly.
It doesn't usually say, "I am arrogant."
It says, "I just know my worth."
It says, "I refuse to let anyone disrespect me."
It says, "That's just how I am."
It says, "I have nothing to apologize for."
It says, "God knows my heart."
And sometimes those statements can express legitimate boundaries or genuine pain.
But sometimes they are simply pride wearing the language of self-respect.
There is a difference between refusing abuse and refusing correction.
There is a difference between standing for truth and insisting that you can never be wrong.
There is a difference between healthy boundaries and punishing someone because they wounded your ego.
Pride blurs those distinctions until every correction feels like persecution and every disagreement feels like an attack.
That's why pride is so dangerous.
It can convince us that repentance is something other people need.
Consider the Pharisee and the tax collector in Luke 18:9–14.
Jesus told this parable specifically to people who trusted in their own righteousness and despised others.
The Pharisee stood praying, thanking God that he was not like other sinners.
He fasted.
He gave tithes.
He had religious discipline.
He could point to visible evidence of devotion.
The tax collector stood at a distance.
He would not even lift his eyes toward heaven.
Instead, he struck his chest and cried:
"God be merciful to me a sinner." (Luke 18:13, KJV)
In Greek, his plea includes the words ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ (hilasthēti moi tō hamartōlō).
It is a plea for God's mercy toward a sinner, with language connected to atonement and reconciliation.
The tax collector wasn't offering God a résumé.
He wasn't comparing himself to someone worse.
He wasn't blaming the devil for his condition.
He was asking for mercy.
And Jesus said it was this man, rather than the Pharisee, who went home justified.
Imagine that.
The man who could list his religious accomplishments was not the example of justification.
The man who knew he desperately needed mercy was.
Because the Gospel does not begin with proving that we are better than others.
It begins with recognizing that we cannot save ourselves.
And I wonder how many of us have become so skilled at sounding righteous that we have forgotten what it feels like to be broken before God.
We know the worship songs.
We know the Bible verses.
We know how to say, "The Lord rebuke you."
But when was the last time we genuinely prayed:
"Lord, show me where I have been proud"?
Not where my spouse has been proud.
Not where my pastor has been proud.
Not where my friends have been proud.
Me.
My attitude.
My words.
My secret contempt.
My defensiveness.
My refusal to apologize.
My desire to win even when winning means hurting someone I love.
That is a different kind of prayer.
Because it's possible to love the idea of spiritual victory while fearing the vulnerability of repentance.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You haven't spoken to a family member in months.
You tell people you've moved on.
But deep down, you're still rehearsing the argument.
Still imagining what you should have said.
Still waiting for the other person to admit they were wrong.
And maybe they really did hurt you.
Maybe your pain is completely legitimate.
Humility does not require pretending wrongdoing never happened. Forgiveness does not automatically restore trust or remove necessary boundaries.
But what if, in the middle of that legitimate pain, God is asking you to examine the bitterness that has begun growing inside you?
What if He is not asking you to excuse their sin, but to stop allowing their sin to govern your heart?
What if the healing you've been praying for begins with surrendering your need to have the final word?
That question hurts.
Especially when we've spent years believing that being right is the same thing as being righteous.
But Jesus never taught that spiritual maturity means winning every confrontation.
Look at Him.
Philippians 2:5–8 calls believers to have the mind of Christ, who humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even death on a cross.
The Greek word ἐταπείνωσεν (etapeinōsen) in Philippians 2:8 means "He humbled."
This is not the humiliation of someone exposed as sinful.
Jesus was without sin.
This is the voluntary humility of the sinless Son who obeyed the Father and gave Himself for sinners.
And here is the part that should bring us to silence.
The only Person who never needed to apologize for sin was willing to suffer for the sins of people who desperately needed forgiveness.
Meanwhile, we sometimes refuse to say three simple words.
"I was wrong."
The Savior humbled Himself.
Yet His followers can become offended when someone corrects them.
The Savior washed His disciples' feet.
Yet we sometimes treat serving others as beneath us.
The Savior prayed for those crucifying Him.
Yet we can spend days nurturing resentment because someone embarrassed us in public.
This is not a reason to despair.
It is a reason to return to Jesus.
Because the same Gospel that exposes our pride also announces the grace that can transform us.
Peter knew something about that transformation.
He was bold.
Passionate.
Quick to speak.
Quick to promise loyalty.
He insisted he would never deny Jesus, even if others fell away.
And then came the courtyard.
The questions.
The fear.
The denials.
The rooster.
And the terrible realization that his confidence in himself had been greater than his understanding of his own weakness.
Luke 22:61–62 records that the Lord turned and looked at Peter, and Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Imagine that moment.
No impressive declaration.
No spiritual speech.
No attempt to explain himself.
Just a broken disciple facing what he had done.
But that was not the end of Peter's story.
After His resurrection, Jesus restored Peter in John 21:15–19 and called him again to care for His sheep and follow Him.
The man who had publicly denied Christ was not beyond Christ's restoring grace.
And later, Peter would write:
There is something profoundly beautiful about that.
The disciple who once trusted his own strength became a shepherd urging believers toward humility.
His failure did not become his final identity.
Jesus rewrote the story.
Not by pretending Peter had never denied Him.
But by meeting a repentant disciple with restoring love and a renewed calling.
That is what grace does.
It does not call pride holiness.
It does not excuse sin.
It does not flatter our egos.
It brings us into the light and leads us back to the Savior.
And perhaps that is the word someone desperately needs today.
You are not beyond restoration because you have been proud.
You are not beyond forgiveness because you have been defensive.
You are not beyond the reach of Christ because you have hurt people while believing you were right.
But do not confuse the availability of grace with permission to remain unchanged.
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could become more sophisticated at defending our sins.
He came to save sinners.
He calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
And through His Spirit, He transforms people who could never transform themselves.
The Hebrew Scriptures speak with remarkable clarity about pride.
Proverbs 16:18 says:
"Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall." (KJV)
The Hebrew word translated "pride" is גָּאוֹן (ga'on), which can refer to majesty or exaltation, but in this warning describes destructive arrogance.
The word translated "destruction" is שֶׁבֶר (shever), meaning breaking, ruin, or collapse.
The proverb warns that arrogance sets a person on a path toward ruin.
It does not teach that every hardship is punishment for pride.
It warns us about the danger of exalting ourselves.
And sometimes that danger appears in places we least expect.
A ministry leader who cannot receive correction.
A worship singer who resents someone else receiving recognition.
A Bible teacher who uses knowledge to humiliate rather than build up.
A believer who treats every disagreement as evidence that others lack discernment.
A Christian who speaks constantly about holiness but rarely demonstrates gentleness.
We can be passionate about defending biblical truth and still become proud in the way we defend it.
Truth matters.
Doctrine matters.
Discernment matters.
But so does the character of the person speaking.
Ephesians 4:15 calls us to speak the truth in love.
Not truth without love.
Not love without truth.
Both.
Because biblical conviction is not permission for cruelty.
And spiritual authority is never a license for arrogance.
Think of the people who have been wounded by Christians who were more interested in being correct than being Christlike.
Some were publicly shamed when they needed patient correction.
Some were dismissed when they tried to explain their pain.
Some were told to stop questioning leaders who themselves refused accountability.
Some walked away from church communities carrying wounds inflicted by people who spoke constantly about God's love.
That should grieve us.
Not because the Gospel has failed.
But because human pride can so terribly misrepresent the One we claim to follow.
And this is where the question becomes deeply personal.
What happens when our children remember our anger more vividly than our prayers?
What happens when our spouse hears us worship Jesus on Sunday but fears approaching us with concerns on Monday?
What happens when our friends know we can quote Scripture but cannot receive a difficult conversation without becoming defensive?
What happens when our public Christianity looks impressive while our private relationships are suffering?
Jesus said in John 13:35:
"By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another." (KJV)
Not merely by the volume of our declarations.
Not by how aggressively we confront the devil.
Not by how many arguments we win online.
By love.
And biblical love is not weak.
Love can confront sin.
Love can establish boundaries.
Love can speak difficult truth.
But love does not delight in humiliating people.
Love does not require every conversation to end with our superiority established.
Love can say, "Please forgive me."
And mean it.
Maybe that is where your next spiritual breakthrough needs to begin.
Not with another accusation.
Not with another explanation of why everyone else is wrong.
But with an honest confession.
"Father, I have been proud."
"Lord, I have used my pain to justify cruelty."
"Jesus, I have demanded grace for myself while withholding mercy from others."
"Forgive me for treating correction like an attack."
"Teach me to love truth more than my own reputation."
And perhaps the hardest prayer of all:
"Lord, even if I am right about what happened, show me where my response has been wrong."
That prayer can change a marriage.
It can reopen an honest conversation between a parent and child.
It can begin repairing a friendship.
It can bring accountability into a ministry.
It can free a believer from the exhausting need to appear perfect.
Not every relationship will be reconciled. Repentance cannot force another person to respond well, and some relationships require distance for safety.
But we can still obey Christ with the part of the story entrusted to us.
Romans 12:18 says:
"If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men." (KJV)
As much as lies in you.
You cannot control another person's repentance.
You cannot force someone to forgive you.
You cannot guarantee that every broken relationship will be restored.
But you can stop using their failures to excuse your own.
And there is freedom in that.
The freedom to admit wrongdoing without believing your entire identity has collapsed.
The freedom to accept correction without feeling worthless.
The freedom to apologize without needing the other person to apologize first.
The freedom to stop performing spiritual strength and start walking in genuine dependence on Jesus.
That is not weakness.
That is what grace begins to produce in a surrendered heart.
And before we go any further, I want to ask you something.
Not for a religious answer.
Not for something impressive.
Just something honest.
When was the last time you admitted you were wrong without immediately explaining why someone else was also at fault?
When was the last time you asked someone you hurt how your actions affected them, and then listened without defending yourself?
When was the last time you welcomed correction because you wanted to become more like Jesus?
If these questions make you uncomfortable, don't rush past them.
Sit with them before God.
Because conviction can be a mercy.
Hebrews 4:12 describes God's Word as living and powerful, discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
And sometimes the Word cuts through the stories we have been telling ourselves.
We thought we were being courageous.
But we were being harsh.
We thought we were defending righteousness.
But we were protecting our reputation.
We thought we were exercising discernment.
But we were nurturing suspicion and contempt.
We thought we were resisting the enemy.
But we were refusing to submit an area of our hearts to God.
And yet, even here, there is hope.
Because Jesus Christ is not waiting for you to manufacture a spotless history before you come to Him.
He already knows the truth.
The hidden jealousy.
The stubbornness.
The unforgiving thoughts.
The pride behind the carefully chosen words.
He knows.
And still, the invitation of the Gospel stands.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
Confess what is true.
Trust in His finished work on the cross and His resurrection.
Receive the mercy you could never earn.
And walk in the newness of life He gives.
First John 1:9 promises:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
Notice what Scripture calls us to do.
Confess.
Not disguise.
Not redirect.
Not minimize.
Confess.
The Greek word ὁμολογῶμεν (homologōmen) means "we confess" or "we acknowledge."
Confession is an honest acknowledgment of sin before God.
It is not informing Him of something He didn't know.
It is ceasing to hide behind our excuses.
And the promise is not that we earn forgiveness by performing enough remorse.
The promise rests upon God's faithfulness and justice, grounded in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
This is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is the fitting response of a sinner who has encountered the truth and mercy of God.
And grace is not the enemy of transformation.
Grace teaches us to renounce ungodliness and live for the Lord, as Titus 2:11–14 declares.
So yes, resist the devil.
Pray.
Stand firm in faith.
Put on the whole armor of God, as Ephesians 6 teaches.
But do not forget that the same Bible which commands spiritual resistance also commands humility, confession, forgiveness, and repentance.
We cannot use one biblical command to escape another.
We cannot rebuke our way out of personal responsibility.
We cannot substitute spiritual vocabulary for obedience.
And we cannot become like Christ while insisting that our pride remain untouched.
Maybe tonight, before you sleep, you need to put down your phone and pray differently.
Maybe you need to stop composing that angry message.
Maybe you need to make a call.
Maybe you need to tell your child, "I should not have spoken to you that way."
Maybe you need to tell your spouse, "I was so focused on proving my point that I stopped listening to your heart."
Maybe you need to tell a brother or sister in Christ, "I corrected you without gentleness, and I am sorry."
Maybe you need to ask a trusted believer to help you recognize the patterns you keep defending.
Or maybe, before any conversation with anyone else, you need to get alone with God.
No audience.
No applause.
No carefully edited testimony.
Just you and the Lord.
And one honest prayer.
"Jesus, I have spent so much time asking You to change the people around me. Please begin with me."
There is no shame in coming to Christ with an honest, repentant heart.
The shame would be continuing to hide when His mercy invites us into the light.
And if this article has exposed something in your heart, I don't want you to leave with mere emotion.
I want you to remember the cross.
Remember the Savior who humbled Himself.
Remember the blood that was shed for sinners.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember that your greatest hope is not your ability to become humble through willpower.
Your hope is Jesus Christ, who saves by grace and works in His people through His Spirit.
The goal is not to become a person who never needs correction.
The goal is to become a disciple who receives correction with humility and returns to Christ in repentance and faith.
That is a life worth pursuing.
And if you are reading this with tears in your eyes because you suddenly recognize how much damage pride has caused, please hear this.
Your story does not have to end with the relationships you damaged, the words you regret, or the years you spent refusing to admit the truth.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
You cannot undo every consequence.
But in Christ, forgiveness is real, transformation is possible, and your past does not have to dictate the direction of your future.
This is the heart behind Gospel Warrior.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not because sin doesn't matter.
But because Jesus is greater than the sin He came to save us from.
Not because our failures are imaginary.
But because His mercy is real.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because the risen Christ calls sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
And if you have made it this far, perhaps this is more than another article passing through your Facebook feed.
Perhaps it is an opportunity to respond to what God has been showing you through His Word.
Don't merely react to this message.
Bring it before the Lord.
You do not have to expose private details to strangers. A simple prayer request is enough.
Someone reading silently may need to know that repentance is not the end of hope.
It can be the beginning of a changed life.
You may never know who among your family, friends, coworkers, or former church companions is quietly wrestling with these very questions.
A single share may place Scripture before someone who would never have searched for a message about pride on their own.

Not because every word here must be remembered, but because the Scriptures we've explored deserve to be revisited, especially on the days when pride begins whispering that we have nothing left to learn.
Because we don't need more religious performances.
We need to keep returning to the truth of God's Word.
And I want to share something personal about the mission behind these messages.
Gospel Warrior exists to help people encounter the Gospel, examine their lives in the light of Scripture, and grow deeper in their walk with Jesus Christ.
We want these resources to continue reaching people who are spiritually hungry, discouraged, confused, wounded, or simply longing to know Christ more deeply.
And that kind of ongoing work benefits from a community willing to support it.
We glorify God through faith in Christ, obedience, worship, love, service, and generosity according to His Word.
Supporting Gospel-centered work can be one meaningful expression of that generosity.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Not a promise that money can secure a blessing.
But an opportunity to participate in work you believe is worth sustaining.
These products are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
But they can serve as reminders of biblical truth, meaningful gifts, and practical ways to help sustain the resources we continue making available.
Your participation matters.
Your prayers matter.
And above all, the truth of Jesus Christ matters.
Because this ministry is not about building a platform that makes people admire us.
It is about pointing people toward the Savior who alone is worthy of our worship.
And perhaps that brings us back to the very question that started this conversation.
Why do we rebuke the devil but refuse to confront our own pride?
Maybe because rebuking an enemy feels easier than admitting our own sin.
Maybe because confronting evil outside us allows us to feel strong, while confessing the evil within us requires humility.
Maybe because we have confused spiritual confidence with personal infallibility.
But Jesus is calling us to something better.
Not a life without spiritual warfare.
A life of submission to God in the middle of it.
Not a life where we never confront darkness.
A life where we also allow God's Word to confront the darkness in our own hearts.
Not a life of endless self-condemnation.
A life of repentance, faith, grace, and growing obedience.
So resist the devil.
But don't resist the correction of your Father.
Stand firm against temptation.
But don't stand stubbornly against the truth.
Fight the good fight of faith.
But don't make war against the very humility Christ is teaching you.
And when you discover pride in your heart, don't run from Jesus.
Run to Him.
He already knows.
He is merciful.
And He is able to transform those who come to Him in faith.
Because the most heartbreaking defeat is not losing an argument to someone else… it is winning every argument while slowly losing the humility to kneel before Jesus.
